items.headline: US military cuts generals, admirals by 20%, Hegseth says
items.snippet: The US defense secretary has also unveiled major changes, including a new drone command and an Elon Musk-led task force to assess the future of warfare.

items.headline: France: Hundreds arrested as student protests escalate
items.snippet: Student protests have grown in scale and intensity, with violent clashes in some places leading to hundreds of arrests and dozens of injuries.

items.headline: Gaza: NGO reports dire camp conditions, says Israel is moving 'Yellow Line'
items.snippet: The Danish Refugee Council alleges that Israel is employing "a policy of protracted displacement" in Gaza. It says the so-called "Yellow Line" is creeping west toward the coast, preventing many from returning home.

items.headline: Five EU states plan first deportation center in Africa for 2027
items.snippet: Greece, Germany, Austria, Denmark and the Netherlands are moving forward with plans to establish deportation centers outside the EU. An African partner country has reportedly already been selected.

items.headline: Flydubai pilot investigated over possible attempt to crash Tel Aviv-bound flight
items.snippet: A Flydubai service from the UAE to Israel made an emergency landing after the copilot stabbed the captain. Eyewitnesses said he attempted to crash the plane before he was subdued by passengers.

items.headline: France's Macron, Spain's Sanchez welcome idea of UK rejoining EU after Burnham remarks
items.snippet: During a visit to Spain, France's Emmanuel Macron said it would be "good news" if the UK moves towards the EU, with Pedro Sanchez also embracing the idea. UK PM Andy Burnham has not ruled out rejoining the bloc.

items.headline: Are the Houthis winning against Saudi Arabia?
items.snippet: It's unclear how the Saudis can defuse the threat presented by the Houthis in next-door Yemen or who they can turn to for help. The US isn't interested, the Europeans are hedging and nobody wants open conflict with Iran.

items.headline: Germany debates alleged antisemitism in the Left Party
items.snippet: The Central Council of Jews in Germany thinks the Left Party is dangerous. Other Jews, however, are showing solidarity with the party. How does that add up?

items.headline: Senegal's Youth Olympics makes Olympics in Africa 'logical'
items.snippet: The Youth Olympics are to be hosted in Africa for the first time ever. The edition in Senegal is also a chance to prove the continent can host a full Olympics in the future.

items.headline: African leaders herald $16B Dangote oil refinery in Kenya
items.snippet: An oil refinery on Kenya's coast is expected to be completed in 40 months, and will process an estimated 700,000 barrels of oil per day. Africa's richest man, Aliko Dangote, will lead the project.

items.headline: Germany raises Deutschlandticket price to €66.80 a month from 2027 under new cost-based formula
items.snippet: A new cost-based formula has pushed up the price of Germany's nationwide public transport pass for 2027.

items.headline: Iran's nuclear program remains shrouded in mystery as the regime debates ditching non-proliferation
items.snippet: Iran's nuclear program is entering a critical phase as Tehran debates dropping out of a nuclear non-proliferation treaty. Satellite images also show activity at known nuclear sites.

items.headline: Lawyer of Junaid Hafeez, a Pakistai scholar imprisoned for 13 years, is hopeful for his release
items.snippet: A former Fullbright scholar, Junaid Hafeez was sentenced to death under Pakistan's controversial blasphemy laws. His family and lawyer told DW there is now hope a court will overturn the conviction.

items.headline: Manchester City Premier League charges: What do they mean?
items.snippet: Since being bought by the UAE in 2008, Manchester City have become one of the world's most successful football clubs. A raft of serious financial charges threatens to undermine this and bring chaos to the Premier League.

items.headline: Servers at Munich's iconic Oktoberfest call for more respect
items.snippet: Oktoberfest is famous the world over for beer, brass band music and Bavarian traditions. But staff at the Wiesn are also reporting incidents of racism and sexism. They're taking a stand against discrimination.

items.headline: Bosnia elections: Polls overshadowed by exhaustion, exodus and geopolitics as ethnic politics eclipse real problems
items.snippet: Bosnia goes to the polls on October 4 to elect several parliaments and presidents. While voters worry about the economy and emigration, the campaign is focused on ethnicity, exposing the country's political paralysis.

items.headline: Is US President Donald Trump right to rename AI as 'Super Intelligence'?
items.snippet: Donald Trump thinks the name artificial intelligence sounds "fake" and has ordered US agencies to use "Super Intelligence" instead. Yet, tech firms and researchers have little reason to play along.

items.headline: Ireland will boycott Eurovision again because of Israel's participation, but the song contest is still expanding.
items.snippet: The 2026 Eurovision Song Contest was marred by boycotts in protest against Israel's participation in the midst of its war on Gaza. It still aims to keep growing.

items.headline: South Korea: Lost shark draws over half a million visitors
items.snippet: The South Korean port of Busan says that a stranded shark has become a major tourist draw. It's also named the ocean predator an honorary ambassador to the city.

items.headline: Germany news: Volkswagen ends collective wage agreements
items.snippet: In an effort to cut costs, automaker Volkswagen terminated most of its collective wage agreements in Germany. This could reignite disputes with employee representatives.

items.headline: El Nino is a 'postcard from the future' — and could cause 451,000 excess heat deaths
items.snippet: The current El Nino could cause 451,000 excess heat deaths. Researchers warn it offers a glimpse of temperatures that may become normal within 20 years.

items.headline: Hungary's reckoning with Orban's corrupt system picks up speed
items.snippet: Hungary's Prime Minister Peter Magyar vowed to dismantle Orban's corrupt networks. High-profile figures are being arrested and many Hungarians are pushing for swift accountability, but the rule of law takes time.

items.headline: South Park satirist pushes for accountability in Cornell gang-rape lawsuit
items.snippet: Writer Toby Morton is using a new website to amplify allegations in a high-profile sexual assault lawsuit involving seven Cornell students. The reopening of the case is causing an outcry on social media.

items.headline: UK PM Burnham seeks 'hope again' at Labour Party conference
items.snippet: Andy Burnham is seeking a delicate balance between optimism and realism at Labour's annual party conference. He promised hope and an end to "politics as usual" but also an "honest conversation" about difficult dilemmas.

items.headline: Albania: As corruption cases multiply, experts question whether the anti-corruption drive is addressing the causes or just the symptoms.
items.snippet: From a former president to the ex-intelligence chief, Albania is prosecuting senior officials at a rate once thought impossible. But do more prosecutions mean less corruption or simply better enforcement?

items.headline: Global trade weathers Iran, Ukraine and Trump's tariffs
items.snippet: Over the past six years, COVID, two wars and Donald Trump's tariffs have shaken world trade. With globalization already stalling, is this a temporary shock or the start of a great reversal?

items.headline: AI: Concern as Germany plans to double data center capacity
items.snippet: Germany is rewriting the rules to attract data center investment from AI companies. But local communities are becoming increasingly skeptical.

items.headline: Spain grows fruit and vegetables for Europe, but it's running out of water
items.snippet: Spain's southern coast produces up to 25% of Europe's fruit and vegetables. But amid intensive farming, climate change and illegal wells, the water it takes to grow them is drying up.

items.headline: UK: US government questions bail for Fairford base suspects
items.snippet: The US government sees "the hand of a foreign actor" in the security scare at RAF Fairford, a hub for US heavy bombers in Europe. Donald Trump criticized the suspects being released on bail amid ongoing investigations.

items.headline: Sicily: Mount Etna ash disrupts Catania flights again
items.snippet: A thick ash cloud from Mount Etna has been disrupting flights to Catania in Sicily for several days. Italy and Europe's most active volcano, Etna has impacted air travel several times this summer.

items.headline: Turkey: Comedian convicted for 'insulting' Erdogan in show
items.snippet: Deniz Goktas was convicted of two of three charges, including "insulting" the president, but was released pending the appeal process. Nominally, Turkey is a secular country with free speech.

items.headline: What do Manchester City's charges mean for German football?
items.snippet: Manchester City have reportedly been found guilty of major financial rule breaches. What does this mean for German football?

items.headline: Germany news: COVID vaccine maker BioNTech to close 3 sites
items.snippet: COVID-19 vaccine maker BioNTech is to close three sites in Germany after efforts to find buyers failed. Meanwhile, Rhine water levels have fallen to record lows after an unusually dry September. DW has more.

items.headline: Diesel prices are surging putting further pressure on Europe
items.snippet: Trucks, farms and industry are powered with diesel. Now prices are soaring due to refinery disruptions, supply shortages and geopolitical tensions. A potential US export ban could make Europe's diesel crunch even worse.

items.headline: Will Jürgen Klopp's charisma be enough for Germany?
items.snippet: After defeat to Greece, Jürgen Klopp faces the first real test of his tenure as coach of Germany's national men's football team. Can his charisma alone push this group forward?

items.headline: Ireland beat Israel 3-0 in Nations League match overshadowed by political controversy
items.snippet: Ireland easily beat Israel in a Nations League fixture that 24 hours earlier appeared in doubt. One Irish player pulled out of the match to express his opposition to Israel's actions in the Gaza Strip.

items.headline: What would Francis of Assisi make of his fame today?
items.snippet: The Catholic saint renounced wealth and fame to become a mendicant friar. Yet throughout history, his teachings and life have inspired popes, Dante and even Mussolini.

items.headline: European cities seek ways of boosting affordable housing
items.snippet: In many major urban centers of Europe, the housing shortage has become an explosive social issue. DW looks into various models that have been put in place across the continent.

items.headline: Germany news: Are Germans giving up their beloved meat and sausages?
items.snippet: Germans used to be all about sausages and meat. While those do remain popular, things seem to be slowly changing. There also are new insights into the economic side of East Germany's espionage DW has more.

items.headline: Backlash over data centers tests Europe's AI ambitions
items.snippet: Massive data centers needed to run AI are triggering protests across Europe. Their operators counter that they boost digital sovereignty and energy independence.

items.headline: Russia expected to intensify hybrid war on Europe
items.snippet: Drone explosions, airspace violations, arson attacks: Poland, Romania, and Moldova are now regularly targeted in Russian attacks against Ukraine. More governments are calling these attacks deliberate acts of aggression.

items.headline: Russian classroom propaganda glorifies dying for your country, students say
items.snippet: The Russian government has stepped up its efforts to spread patriotic propaganda in schools. DW spoke to students about textbooks that portray the West as hostile and promote sacrifice for the nation.

items.headline: DW shows solidarity with Georgians' commitment to democracy
items.snippet: Cultural and media professionals in Georgia remain under threat. A DW panel brings together insiders who share their hopes and fears.

items.headline: 'Lithuanian skies are NATO skies': DW speaks with Lithuanian premier Mindaugas Sinkevicius
items.snippet: In a DW interview, Prime Minister Mindaugas Sinkevicius discussed threats to Lithuania from Russia and Belarus, NATO's need for stronger air defense and why military spending alone cannot ensure security.

items.headline: Bundesliga, other top European leagues call for major FIFA reforms
items.snippet: The Bundesliga and three other leading European football leagues have said major reforms to world-governing body FIFA are "essential." However, they stopped short of calling for the resignation of boss Gianni Infantino.

items.headline: How Bulgaria become a global leader in battery storage and what this means for the country's grid and energy market?
items.snippet: In under two years, Bulgaria has become one of the world's most battery-intensive energy markets. Can the surge last — and what will it mean for conventional power generators?

items.headline: Italy to ban burqa in schools, limit foreign pupils
items.snippet: Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni’s government has passed new school rules capping the number of students who don't speak fluent Italian and banning face coverings.

items.headline: Jürgen Klopp starts Germany job with shaky Netherlands draw
items.snippet: A late Netherlands goal denied Jürgen Klopp a win in his first match as Germany coach. The former Liverpool and Borussia Dortmund boss has big ambitions, but the game showed he's going to need more time to achieve them.

items.headline: Three-way battle for power in world chess: Who will be elected FIDE president in Samarkand?
items.snippet: The era of Russian presidents is coming to an end at the World Chess Federation (FIDE). Two Germans and one Kazakh are up for election. Among the issues at play are money, Kremlin influence, and unanswered questions.

items.headline: After several difficult years, economists now expect German economy to grow
items.snippet: Germany's economy is growing again, but recovery remains on shaky ground. High government spending is keeping the economy afloat, while energy prices, a shortage of skilled workers and debt continue to weigh on it.

items.headline: Political psychology: Why extremist parties are thriving and what democratic politicians can do against it
items.snippet: Far-right and far-left parties are celebrating success after success, leaving moderate politicians in the dust and worrying many Germans. Political psychology helps us understand what's behind growing polarization.

items.headline: Could flattering AI make humanity turn on itself?
items.snippet: A study shows chatbots mirror users' politics, part of a broader tendency known as AI sycophancy. Researchers fear this could deepen polarization.

items.headline: Germany news: Berlin officially withdraws Olympics bid
items.snippet: Berlin's decision to withdraw its Olympic bid means that only Munich and the western Rhine/Ruhr region are left in the running as potential Olympic hosts. DW has more.

items.headline: Czech PM Andrej Babis reiterates importance of NATO for his country but rejects calls to increase defense spending
items.snippet: The US and NATO want Czechia to spend more on defense. Czech Prime Minister Andrej Babis says Prague cannot afford faster increases, despite growing warnings about the threat from Russia.

items.headline: 'Pope fever' takes hold as Pope Leo visits France
items.snippet: Pope Leo XIV is expected to draw huge crowds during his visit to France. As part of his trip, he's also set to address Europe's future and some of the challenges ahead.
